Baka-dālbhya
(‘Baka, a descendant of Dalbha’)
------------------------------------------
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (1.2.13) mentions one बक-दाल्भ्य, as a sage who had realized the प्राण (the chief vital air in the body and the deity presiding over it) through the singing of the उद्गीथ (a part of the sāma hymn). He was the उद्गातृ priest in the sacrifice performed by the Naimiśīyas and successfully got them what they wanted.
The Jaminīya Upaniṣad Brāhmaṇa states (1.9.2) that बक-दाल्भ्य restrained इन्द्र from harming the Ājakeśins (mem-bers of a particular family).
The Vāmanapurāṇa (ch. 39) gives the story of a sage बक-दाल्भ्य who was about to destroy the kingdom of a ruler, धृतराष्ट्र by name, through a sacrifice. The latter meanwhile realized his mistake—he had slighted the sage once—made amends for the same, pleased the sage and got back all that he had lost.
It is rather difficult to say whether all these बक-dālbhyas were one and the same. The possibility cannot be ruled out.

Baka
------------------------------------------
Baka or Bakāsura was a rākṣasa (demon) who lived near the small town एकचक्रनगर. Since he used to attack the town and eat up the human beings there, the residents of the town had made an agreement with him to supply ड़ोओद् and one adult human being every day from among them, by turns. When the Pāṇḍavas were living there after being exiled, भीम (the second of the Pāṇḍava brothers) managed to kill him, thus ridding the town of a great menace (vide Mahā-bhārata, आदिपर्व-163).
The Bhāgavata (10.12) mentions of another demon बक (in the form of a crane) who was killed by कृष्ण.

Bakapañcaka
(‘pentad related to the crane’)
------------------------------------------
Vratas or religious vows and observances are an integral part of हिन्दुइस्म् in practice. They are common even today. Among the several such vratas, ‘Baka-pañcaka’ is one listed by religious digests. The five days from Kārttika śukla ekādaśi (eleventh day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika, generally falling in November) to pūrṇimā (the full-मोओन् day) are so called since it was believed that even a बक or a crane will not eat meat in these days. Hence, abstaining from eating meat during these five days is the main discipline expected of the votary.
See also VRATAS.
